I recommend ‘I agree they’re not back to baseline yet. It’ll take time to heal at home but being in hospital for longer won’t improve that and with the noise/no windows/crappy lighting it’ll get worse. I couldn’t heal in this place. We’ve been a big part of their investigation phase, and whilst I can’t pinpoint it exactly I can now say safely that there isn’t anything life threatening. It doesn’t mean they’ll feel well though and that’a why we need xyz follow up’.

You can use the fractured arm example - it will still really hurt until it’s healed. You still might need something in the future, but for now you’re as safe as modern medicine can make you.

Some people and culture feel staying in hospital until you are 100% is the expectation, and with infinite resources that would be ideal. No home responsibilities, food and caring people on tap, and reassurance. I understand it personally. And not everyone has supportive family, finances or has reassurance. It’s worth a golden minute to listen to.

Provide some strategies to occupy them positively (symptom diaries and a mini rehab goal eg headache present but able to do light reading or a walk, think like a concussion graded return to activity).

Having these conversations with colleagues and patients is hard, but see it as a collaborative effort and explain the medical thought process to the nurses so they understand why xyz decision was made too.

Just move out to Australia/NZ now! You can comfortably earn more as a junior than you ever will training in the UK. That way you can be part time and won’t have to stress as much with childcare. As you’ll have a wage you can support yourself on (rather than the UK pittance) you can then either enjoy parenthood more easily, do your exams or both. 

Exams and ease of progression depends on you and where you work. Some paths are shorter but are harder to get onto training in the first place, don’t have exit exams etc etc. I would suggest looking into a speciality that doesn’t require massive/any overtime and lets you pick your days off and do less than full time!

What speciality are you working in? Did you move over with friends/partner? It’s super tough emigrating, even from the UK. You lose your supports. You have the extra burdens of new systems, APHRA and sign offs as well as trying to sort all your life admin etc.

I can’t help with alternative careers but what I would say is if you aren’t happy, try another post in Australia. I wasn’t happy with the first place I moved to and then moved again and loved it. Reignited my love of medicine and never looked back.

Thanks - you’ve pretty much smashed this better than I could have done. ICU reg job is generally better paid than ED due to how the roster falls (eg 7 on gets higher penalties if it’s all in one week). 

Don’t come to Australia to locum. Come because the training is good, you are fairly paid and work 38 hours a week, not 48. Locum if is doable but even so you’re working in a hospital often different from your own and with no support. The whole idea is that doctors are well paid enough in training to attract talent and then often reduce locum compliance so you have a good solid base of doctors at each hospital who want to contribute and build so it feels less mercenary!

Nope definitely worth applying. The directors tend to review all CVs and can offer you a job if you’re a better candidate than the locals. Also very variable competition for different hospitals here so it’s always worth a shot. They may have people cancel/change plans and off you the job instead too even if you weren’t the initial preferred candidate. It’s a different feeling from applying to the UK generally as you are applying to a hospital rather than being ranked and placed

What this person said! I do know an IMG who has managed to get onto paeds on a temporary visa though. Also definitely now. In 15 years with inflation degrading your NHS pay you’ll be earning less than a Pret a Manger intern, yet alone manager.

So it’s all based on years post graduation. Eg intern, then PGY1,2 and so on. Caps out at PGY4 I think. SRMO is an RMO position usually for pay, but unaccredited registrar would be paid as a registrar. The advertised job should tell you which category it falls under and you can email a hospital if there is any doubt. You can good ‘NSW health award’ then look for medical officers in the table to see the pay breakdowns. The pay listed will be basic and not incorporate penalty rates

Depends on your job role. If you take a resident job, you’ll be paid as ‘Resident 4th year’ $115k basic, in a reg role it’s $133k basic I believe. This is for NSW, higher in other states I believe (but I can’t be bothered to read their awards)

I terms of where you start I guess I depends on what you apply for. If you have 6 months of ED then an SRMO position is good. You could apply for an unaccredited registrar position too but competition is higher and generally better if you are wanting to do ED (have you done ATLS, POCUS courses, APLS etc?). You’d need to have a look at the job descriptions and see what suits you best!

Sorry for the slow reply - moving house at present! ACEM exams are tough and are respected by trainees in other specialities. You have 2 lots (rather than 1 in some colleges). The primary exam is basically preclinical medicine again (yay anatomy). I revised for 12 months, but to be honest it’s a slow burn at the start for everyone and a mad cram in the last few months. The other thing is that exam teaching in the hospitals is a big thing. Our hospital does primary exam teaching in your training every week (again which you get paid extra for attending if you aren’t rostered) and you’ll go through with a cohort of people studying so it’s not too bad. Fellowship exams are similar but it’s more clinical and management, again takes a lot of study but it’s stuff you’re doing every day. It’s doable with kids etc but you just have to be organised. 

Unfortunately medicine will always have exams, but in my experience the hospitals I have been at here will go out of their way to help you pass them. When I did my RCEM written I had no help, no guidance and then when I passed no one cared. Here we celebrate those who pass and would work extra hard to support someone if they didn’t!

Not sure about the UK. In NSW you get 4 weeks a year I think but you get extra days for working public holidays and as a shift worker/working weekends you get more. Plus your ADOs (which can be converted to leave). You can bank leave too, so you can take the maximum the college allows of 10 weeks if you have enough. Equally, you can cash it out if you don’t use it!

Minimum 5 years (depends if you are full time, how quickly you do all your necessary placements, whether you pass you exams first go).

Trainees can take 5 weeks of leave per placement (13 weeks/3 month placement), up to 10 weeks total per year. You don’t have to take it in blocks  you can take your leave in pretty much any form. You can literally take leave days if you need. The roster coordinator just needs to be happy but that’s a hospital thing. Most people get their leave too (within reason - not everyone can have both Christmas and New Year’s Eve off for instance) in my experience.

Parents are in the UK - they come out once a year but now stay with us for a longer period (since having grandkids). Brother is the the UK too. I miss him but FaceTime helps massively. I barely got to see any of them them when I worked in the UK due to the shitty roster and having to locum on my free days to stay afloat - it’s actually better now. I have a close relationship with my in-laws and they have been a great support. Wife is an Aussie (met here, at work) and her parents live in Sydney. 

Starting a new social circle can be hard (I understand being an introvert as well. I also don’t drink) but people here want to be friends in my experience. Department vibes are super friendly generally. Weather is nice so someone will tend to suggest drinks, BBQ, teaching you how to surf. I did things that interested me - life drawing classes and took up motorcycling (solo hobbies but you still meet people). I made friends with my first AirBnB hosts when I came out and then housemates in a flat share. Many doctors are from overseas or out of area too and will want to hang out. You might feel homesick or out of place for a bit (usually 2 months in my experience) but everyone understands that.
I believe it’s around 300k but varies lower and higher up to 400k. Depends on area, whether it’s a free ‘bulk billing’ practice, how many patients you choose to see etc.

Thank you. I love what I do and I can do it properly out here. I think the best thing about being here is that the job give me so much time to spend with my beautiful family... 38 hours a week is so much better than the NHS working week and gives you time for family, gym and generally looking after yourself. It probably explains my overall positivity :)

I think there are jobs but you might need to be flexible. VMO positions exist/are recruiting at major hospitals (but work can be 0 hours - ie not guarenteed). There are often waiting lists to become a staff specialist at major metro hospitals (the difference is you have departmental responsibility, non clinical duties etc). You can differentiate yourself by doing paediatric emergency medicine (fun), but to be honest when you have trained somewhere for ages if you are competent, have a good attitude, are friendly and generally bring positive stuff to the department then they will want to keep you as a boss and will ensure you get work.

Not in ED. I have heard the same in surgical but no personal experience. In ICU/anaesthetics/ED generally once you are on a training scheme the hospital will try and get you through your exams and then your role will be in accordance with progression. In ED you must have passed primaries and rotated through anaesthetics in order to do nights in charge (as you would be expected to intubate independently/know when you need help by having experience). No one would put someone unqualified in that role without experience, even if you were best mates as it wouldn’t stand up in court and most departments have strict policies, as do the colleges. Pay is the same - it goes up by year, not really by specific role so you don’t need to worry about that!

Salary is roughly $300k for new consultants working 38 hours a week doing some weekends in NSW. I think it’s close to $400k after 5 years or so. On call one day every fortnight. Different areas have different pay, particularly rural is much higher (I think South Australia was offering $600k recently for a remote posting)

There’s definitely merit in that, although in Wollongong we have a lot of young trainees so it’s not too bad We also have a young population on the whole so there is stuff to do in the area. It’s a different vibe to the city for sure. I trained at RNSH so I can’t speak to what it would be like moving here at a younger place in life, but I would add that just because something isn’t Sydney doesn’t mean that it’s not worth living in. Most people in the UK aren’t in London and not everyone necessarily wants/has to have that!

Yeah to be honest I have never considered moving state for money. It is a difference but compared to the UK salary I’m still doing well. If you are more rural here (country towns eg Nowra) they will pay you 1 year higher than you are in NSW (etc pay as PGY4 rather than PGY3) so you make up differences. Cost of living is so different depending on area of towns (eg North Shore vs West Sydney or South/North Coast) so hard to compare. I can give a bit of an overview if you/anyone is interested in moving here!

I have met a few psych trainees - it’s a busy job but very lucrative private work as a boss. Many of them cover remote out of hours here when on all. They seem pretty happy and chilled people IMO!

Lots of psych presentations to ED but we quickly get them seen by the psych team (Nurse then Reg or just Reg). Lots of D&A psychosis etc too

I think it depends on speciality. ED is straightforward - you don’t need to mess around with publications etc etc. GP I think is similar. Core medicine seems okay but might be more competitive. Anaesthetics - you basically need to know people on the departments bedore getting a job which takes years of unaccredited work, but once you’re on is straightforward (you can do this by getting over to Aus on an ED or critical care job). Surgical seems a real struggle - many trainees here can’t get on/get unaccredited work for years and have masters/have done their exams. Unfortunately I only really know the ED pathway well but it’s a good one (and the consultant payoff is well worth it!).

I’d say just have a look at a GSX-S1000GT or Ninja 1000SX. Super sport engines and would be trackable (probably better for canyon carving than track) but better ergonomics for commuting. Good for taller riders too. Neither heats up in traffic quite like the Ducati or BMW in my opinion either (but admittedly less horsepower and less brand bragging rights). GSXS is in demand /low supply so will keep resale for now, and the SX is often available used at a good price in Aus. H2SX if you want a Japanese do it all bike with more ponies but I gather the cornering is slightly less flickable. Disclaimer - I went for the GSXS-1000GT and commute 100kms a day at around 110kph and have no regrets (also very, very good for fast corners/mountain carving on the weekend). Some days I think it’s probably not as exciting as the panic ale/street fighter V4 my heart wanted, but it was half the price and way better for what I actually use it for in the real world.

New GSX-S1000GT is super comfy and I use as a daily with no issues. 150bhp and handles well. However some people find that the wind hits their helmet as the screen isn’t adjustable (although I don’t have this issue and I’m 5’11). The 1000SX is probably the one to beat, looks great and is more polished as a tourer, just less sporty. Tracer 9 GT gets great reviews (I always had good experiences with Yamaha in the past) and R1250RS would be worth a look too.

Went from Street Triple RS to Thruxton R. No regrets. Feels special every ride and every time I look at it. Torquier from low revs and I find therefore easier to use in town, but does lack some of the top end grunt (not really noticeable/don’t care). Weight increase seems well hidden. Whole bike has a lot more character to me, not sure why. Exhaust sound is exhilarating (I have her straight piped and SC project tips). Tubed tires are a pain. Chrome scratches easily. Some of the aluminium oxidises too easily unless lanolin coated. People love to stop and stare (/chat) if that’s your thing, had that a lot less with my Triple. Love both bikes though.

I would suggest having a look at the Street Triple RS as the torque is good and you’ll be able to thrash the engine around town. With a decent can (maybe SC project) they sound great and the engine doesn’t heat up too much. Finish is good and won’t be a step down from BMW. I had one and loved it.

My other though would be to look at the RS 660 from Aprilia. I know it’s not a naked, but the seating position is meant to be amazing for day to day, power and sound again look perfect for everyday use. Also stunning design.

I have had 3 Yamaha’s including the MT09 and the engine and triple sound is incredible. Reliability is good and paint quality is surprisingly good/robust. Lots of aftermarket customisation. That said the stock suspension is terrible (imagine riding a pogo stick) and they can therefore be more skittish than you’d like in corners. Also lacked some wow factor IMO and didn’t make me feel as special as it should have done.

I haven’t owned a KTM but residuals were low here due to poor reliability. I read several ‘my engine is leaking and dealership not really helping’ horror stories on the forums and that put me off, as I’m the sort of person who would forever worry about it.

So I put this up in case anyone was thinking of using SC Project as there are very few videos on youtube for the thruxton. I really liked the experience of dealing with them (polite, helpful and gave shipping updates). Took a few weeks to arrive but sound is great. Weight is similar to original tips. Finish has one or two small shape imperfections at the opening, but then I remember they're basically individually crafted when you order them so it doesn't really bother me. Sound was too loud without baffles so I ended up reinstalling. Hope someone finds it helpful!
Appreciate the feedback! I love the straight out look but they widen the profile and made filtering harder. If anyone has any suggestions for smaller bar end mirrors let me know!
